t: 3509. Maximum Product of Subsequences With an Alternating Sum Equal to K
o: Pick a non-empty subsequence whose even-position elements minus odd-position elements equals k, maximizing the product subject to product ≤ limit. Since nums[i] ≤ 12 and limit ≤ 5000, the set of achievable (alternating-sum, product) states is small enough to explore with a hash-set DP: process elements one by one, and for each reached state try appending the new element at an even slot (+v) or odd slot (−v).
k: State = (current alternating difference, current product); both dimensions are bounded (diff ∈ [−1800, 1800], product ≤ 5000).
Each new element branches into two parities: (d+v, p·v) and (d−v, p·v), pruned when the product exceeds limit.
Zeros collapse the product to 0 but still flip parity for subsequent elements, so they must flow through the same transition rather than being skipped.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash-set DP over (difference, product) states
a.i: Maintain a dictionary/set of reachable states. Seeding happens implicitly: for each element we add its two singleton states. After processing all elements, the answer is the maximum product among states with difference exactly k. Pruning products above limit keeps the state space tiny in practice.
s: Initialize an empty set of (diff, product) states.
For each value v: collect new states — singletons (v, v) and (−v, v) if v ≤ limit — plus, from every existing state, (d+v, p·v) and (d−v, p·v) whenever p·v ≤ limit.
Scan final states for diff == k and return the maximum product, or −1 if none.
a.t: O(n·S) where S is the number of reachable (diff, product) states — small because products are capped at limit = 5000

w: Explain the state-space argument in interviews: products are bounded by limit ≤ 5000 and differences by 150·12 = 1800, so although the worst case looks big, pruning keeps it tractable — this is the intended solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that a zero element still occupies a position (parity shift), forgetting singleton seeding (the subsequence must be non-empty), and returning the capped product rather than skipping over-limit states. Edge cases: k outside [−1800, 1800] → immediately −1; limit = 1 restricts to subsequences of 0s and 1s. Follow-up: count qualifying subsequences, or return the lexicographically smallest one.
